angle: A structure so vast it breaks the universe's rule of uniformity, but might just be statistical noise.

claims.claim: The structure is named the Huge-LQG or Huge Large Quasar Group.
The structure measures about 4 billion light-years across.
It would take light 4 billion years to cross the structure.
The discovery was led by Roger G. Clowes.
The team was from the University of Central Lancashire.
The structure is located in the constellation Leo.
The discovery challenges the Cosmological Principle.
Cosmological theory suggests structures should not exceed 370 Megaparsecs.
The structure is 1600 times larger than the distance from the Milky Way to Andromeda.
Quasars are the nuclei of galaxies from the early universe.
Data came from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey.
The quasars have an average redshift of approximately 1.3.
The existence of the structure is disputed as a possible false positive.
Results were published in Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society.

disputed: Whether the Huge-LQG is a real physical structure or a statistical artifact; Clowes et al. claim reality supported by Mg II absorbers, while Nadathur argues it is a false positive from random distribution simulations.
The specific homogeneity scale limit; sources cite 370 Mpc, 260/h Mpc, or 130 Mpc/h depending on the definition used.
Whether the structure supersedes others; only one source mentions it was superseded by the Hercules–Corona Borealis Great Wall.
reason: Sources provide over 16 verified claims with dual-site confirmation, supporting a 45-second narrative on size, discovery, and controversy.
story: In 2013, astronomers led by Roger Clowes from the University of Central Lancashire found the Huge-LQG, a structure of 73 quasars in Leo. It spans 4 billion light-years, taking light itself 4 billion years to cross. This size challenges the Cosmological Principle, which assumes the universe looks the same everywhere at large scales. Theory suggests structures shouldn't exceed 370 megaparsecs, but this one hits 1200 megaparsecs. That's 1600 times the distance to Andromeda. Built from quasar nuclei powered by supermassive black holes, it was mapped using Sloan Digital Sky Survey data at redshift 1.3. However, later analysis suggests it might be a statistical false positive. Simulations show random quasar distributions can mimic such clusters. While some data supports its reality, the debate continues. Published in Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society, it remains a scale breaker, testing the limits of cosmic uniformity.
